questions.stem: Doug is choosing a software development life-cycle model for use in a project he is leading to develop a new business application. He has clearly defined requirements and would like to choose an approach that places an early emphasis on developing comprehensive documentation. He does not have a need for the production of rapid prototypes or iterative improvement. Which model is most appropriate for this scenario?
questions.explanation: The waterfall model uses an approach that develops software sequentially, spending quite a bit of time up front on the development and documentation of requirements and design. The spiral and Agile models focus on iterative development and are appropriate when requirements are not well understood or iterative development is preferred. DevOps is an approach to integrating development and operations activities and is not an SDLC model.
optionNotes: Incorrect. Agile delivers working software in short iterations and favors working code over heavy documentation. Doug has clear requirements and doesn't need iteration, so Agile is a poor fit.

Correct. Waterfall runs sequentially and puts a lot of upfront effort into documenting requirements and design. That suits Doug's well-defined requirements and his need for early, thorough documentation without prototypes.

Incorrect. The spiral model repeats cycles that each produce a prototype, and it works best when requirements are unclear. Doug has explicitly said he doesn't need prototypes or iterative improvement.
Incorrect. DevOps is a way of integrating development and operations activities. It is not an SDLC model, so it can't serve as Doug's life-cycle choice.

questions.stem: Which individual bears the ultimate responsibility for data protection tasks?
questions.explanation: The data owner is a senior manager who bears ultimate responsibility for data protection tasks. The data owner typically delegates this responsibility to one or more data custodians.
optionNotes: Correct. The data owner is a senior manager who holds ultimate responsibility for protecting the data, even after handing the day-to-day work to custodians.
Incorrect. The data custodian is given the day-to-day protection tasks by the owner. The owner can hand off the work but not the ultimate responsibility, so it stays with the owner.
Incorrect. A user accesses data to do their job and must follow security policy. A user has no ownership role and no ultimate responsibility for protecting the data.
Incorrect. An auditor reviews and checks whether controls and policies are implemented correctly. An auditor gives independent assurance but is not responsible for protecting the data.

questions.stem: Carla is conducting a web application security test and would like to automatically generate input that is used to test the application. Which of the following tools would be best suited for this purpose?
questions.explanation: Fuzz testing tools are designed to provide invalid or unexpected input to applications, testing for vulnerabilities like format string vulnerabilities, buffer overflow issues, and other problems. A static analysis relies on examining code without running the application or code and thus would not fill forms as part of a web application. Brute-force tools attempt to bypass security by trying every possible combination for passwords or other values. A white box is a type of penetration test where the testers have full knowledge of the environment.
optionNotes: Incorrect. Static analysis looks at source code without running the application, so it never sends generated input to a live web app or fills in its forms.
Incorrect. White-box describes how much the tester knows (full knowledge of the environment or internal code). It is a testing approach, not a tool that automatically generates input.
Incorrect. Brute-force tools try every possible combination of passwords or other values to get past security. They do not create varied, unexpected input to test how an application behaves.
Correct. Fuzz testing tools automatically feed invalid or unexpected input to an application to find flaws such as buffer overflows and format string vulnerabilities.

questions.stem: Warren's organization recently completed a massive phishing awareness campaign, and he would like to measure its effectiveness. Which of the following tools would best provide this measurement?
questions.explanation: Warren could use a survey or third-party assessment to evaluate the effectiveness of the campaign, but the best evidence would be provided by a phishing simulation where the organization measures user responses to simulated phishing attacks. Code reviews would not be useful in evaluating the effectiveness of antiphishing campaigns.
optionNotes: Incorrect. A survey shows what users say they think or know. It can't show whether they actually avoid clicking real phishing lures, so it's weaker evidence than a simulation.

Correct. A phishing simulation sends realistic fake phishing emails and records how users really respond, such as click and report rates. That gives the most direct evidence of whether the awareness campaign changed behavior.
Incorrect. Code review checks application source code for flaws. It has nothing to do with how employees behave, so it can't measure an anti-phishing awareness campaign.
Incorrect. A third-party assessment could evaluate the program, but it usually reviews materials and processes. It's less direct than measuring how users actually respond to simulated attacks.

questions.stem: Which one of the following controls would be most effective in detecting zero-day attack attempts?
questions.explanation: Anomaly-based intrusion detection systems may identify a zero-day vulnerability because it deviates from normal patterns of activity. Signature-based detection methods would not be effective because there are no signatures for zero-day vulnerabilities. Strong patch management would not be helpful because, by definition, zero-day vulnerabilities do not have patches available. Full-disk encryption would not detect an attack because it is not a detective control.
optionNotes: Incorrect. Signature-based IDS only matches known attack patterns. A zero-day exploit has no signature yet, so this approach wouldn't flag it.
Correct. Anomaly-based IDS learns a baseline of normal activity and alerts on deviations. That lets it catch new, unknown zero-day attack attempts that have no signature.
Incorrect. By definition, no vendor patch exists yet for a zero-day vulnerability. Patch management is also preventive rather than detective.
Incorrect. Full-disk encryption protects the confidentiality of data at rest. It isn't a detective control and can't spot attack attempts.

questions.stem: Rob believes that an individual he met on an online forum used unapproved resources to cheat on the CISSP exam. He has evidence to back up his claim. Which one of the following statements is most correct?
options: Rob may report this situation to ISC2 as a violation of the Code of Ethics.
Rob does not have standing to report this situation to ISC2 unless he is an employer of the individual in question.
Rob does not have standing to report this situation to ISC2 unless he holds a professional license or certification that includes a code of ethics.
Rob does not have standing to report this situation to ISC2 unless he is a member of ISC2 or holds an ISC2 certification.
questions.explanation: Whether Rob has standing to report this situation to ISC2 depends upon the canon(s) violated by the activity. This behavior violates canon II, “Act honorably, honestly, justly, responsibly, and legally.” Any member of the public may file a claim under canons I or II. Only an employer or someone with a contracting relationship with the individual may file a complaint under canon III. Anyone who is certified or licensed as a professional and subscribes to a code of ethics as part of that licensure or certification is eligible to file a canon IV complaint.
optionNotes: Correct. Cheating violates canon II (act honorably, honestly, justly, responsibly, and legally), and any member of the public may file a complaint under canons I or II.
Incorrect. Standing as an employer or contracting party matters only for canon III complaints. This case falls under canon II, which anyone in the public can report.
Incorrect. Holding a professional license or certification with its own code of ethics is needed only for canon IV complaints. It isn't required here because cheating violates canon II.
Incorrect. No canon requires the person complaining to be an ISC2 member or certification holder. Canon I and II complaints are open to any member of the public.

questions.stem: Which one of the following components should be included in an organization's emergency response guidelines?
options: Secondary response procedures for incident responders
Activation procedures for the organization's cold sites
questions.explanation: The emergency response guidelines should include the immediate steps an organization should follow in response to an emergency situation. These include immediate response procedures, a list of individuals who should be notified of the emergency, and secondary response procedures for incident responders. They do not include long-term actions such as activating business continuity protocols, ordering equipment, or activating disaster recovery sites.
optionNotes: Correct. Emergency response guidelines cover the immediate steps taken in an emergency: immediate response procedures, a notification list, and secondary response procedures for incident responders.
Incorrect. Business continuity protocols are long-term actions that keep operations running. They belong in the BCP, not in guidelines for the immediate emergency response.
Incorrect. Activating a cold site or other disaster recovery site is a longer-term step in the DRP. It is not part of the immediate emergency response.
Incorrect. Ordering replacement equipment is a longer-term recovery task, so emergency response guidelines leave it out. They focus on the first actions and who to notify.

questions.stem: When Jim enters his organization's data center, he has to use a smartcard and code to enter and is allowed through one set of doors. The first set of doors closes, and he must then use his card again to get through a second set, which locks behind him. What type of control is this, and what is it called?
options: A physical control; a one-way trapdoor
A logical control; a dual-swipe authorization
A directive control; a one-way access corridor
A preventive access control; an access control vestibule
questions.explanation: An access control vestibule (or mantrap) uses two sets of doors, only one of which can open at a time. An access control vestibule is a type of preventive access control, although its implementation is a physical control.
optionNotes: Incorrect. It is implemented physically, but "one-way trapdoor" isn't a real security term. The correct name for interlocking double doors is an access control vestibule (mantrap).

Incorrect. Logical controls are technical controls such as passwords or ACLs on systems. Even though Jim swipes his card twice, a double door that physically stops tailgating is not a logical control, and "dual-swipe authorization" isn't a standard term.
Incorrect. Directive controls, such as policies or signs, tell people what to do. They don't physically stop entry. "One-way access corridor" also isn't the recognized name for a mantrap.

Correct. Two sets of doors where only one can open at a time make an access control vestibule (mantrap). It is a preventive access control that blocks tailgating, even though it is built as a physical control.

questions.stem: Bill implemented RAID level 5 on a server that he operates using a total of three disks. How many disks may fail without the loss of data?
questions.explanation: RAID level 5 is also known as disk striping with parity. It uses three or more disks, with the equivalent of one disk containing parity information used to restore data to another disk in the event of failure. When used with three disks, RAID 5 is able to withstand the loss of a single disk.
optionNotes: Incorrect. RAID 5 keeps parity data, so it can rebuild the contents of one failed disk. Zero fault tolerance describes RAID 0, which stripes data with no parity.
Correct. RAID 5 stripes data with parity, and the parity takes up the space of one disk. With three disks, the array survives one disk failure because the lost data can be rebuilt from parity.
Incorrect. Surviving two failed disks needs dual parity (RAID 6) or mirroring. RAID 5 has only single parity, so a second failure loses data.
Incorrect. If all three disks fail, nothing is left to rebuild from. No RAID level survives losing every disk in the array.

questions.stem:
Match the following numbered system and organization controls (SOC) levels to their matching lettered SOC report descriptions:
SOC levels:
1. SOC 1, Type 1
2. SOC 1, Type 2
3. SOC 2
4. SOC 3

(Arrange the options in the order of the numbered items 1–4.)
options: A general use report that reports on controls related to compliance and/or operations

A report that provides predefined, standard benchmarks for controls involving confidentiality, availability, integrity, and privacy of a system and the information it contains, generally for restricted use

A report that provides an assessment of the risk of material misstatement of financial statement assertions affected by the service organization's processing and that includes a description of the service auditor's tests of the controls and the results of the tests and their effectiveness

A report that provides the auditor's opinions of financial statements about controls at the service organization and that includes a report on the opinion on the presentation of the service organization's system as well as suitability of the controls
questions.explanation:
The SOC levels match the report descriptions as follows:
1. SOC 1, Type 1: D. A report that provides the auditor's opinions of financial statements about controls at the service organization and that includes a report on the opinion on the presentation of the service organization's system as well as suitability of the controls
2. SOC 1, Type 2: C. A report that provides an assessment of the risk of material misstatement of financial statement assertions affected by the service organization's processing and that includes a description of the service auditor's tests of the controls and the results of the tests and their effectiveness
3. SOC 2: B. A report that provides predefined, standard benchmarks for controls involving confidentiality, availability, integrity, and privacy of a system and the information it contains, generally for restricted use
4. SOC 3: A. A general use report that reports on the effectiveness of controls related to compliance and/or operations
optionNotes: Goes with item 4, SOC 3. SOC 3 is the general-use report on controls related to compliance and/or operations, so it can be shared publicly.
Goes with item 3, SOC 2. SOC 2 uses predefined benchmarks for confidentiality, availability, integrity and privacy, and it is generally for restricted use.
Goes with item 2, SOC 1 Type 2. It describes the auditor's tests of the controls, the test results and how effective the controls were, which are the features that set Type 2 apart from Type 1.
Goes with item 1, SOC 1 Type 1. It gives an opinion on how the system is presented and whether the controls are suitably designed, but includes no testing of how effective they were.
